1. Motivation and background

1. Where we treat matters when an intervention spills over

0.5 mintalk-only
none (title slide)
Slide text
Title, authors (Walther, Habib, Simpson, Lin), UNC Biostatistics, date.
Notes
One sentence of purpose. We are planning how to choose which community colleges receive an SUD-prevention education program first, and the choice affects how well a trial can measure the program's effect.

2. Neighbors share more than a border

1 minprelim
none (two short examples with icons)
Slide text
Bed nets in northern Ghana lowered child mortality in nearby untreated villages. School deworming in Kenya helped untreated children near treated schools. When treatment reaches neighbors, a simple treated-versus-control comparison can understate the effect.
Notes
Spillover breaks the usual cluster-trial assumption that one cluster's outcome ignores its neighbors' assignments. Cite Binka 1998 and Miguel and Kremer 2004 on the slide footer.

3. Analysis methods exist, design guidance is thin

0.75 mintechnical
none (a two-column contrast: analysis-stage tools vs design-stage choices)
Slide text
Spatial models can separate direct and spillover effects after the trial. Few studies say which clusters to treat before the trial starts. Our earlier small-grid study (BMC Medical Research Methodology) compared block-stratified and simple random allocation.
Notes
Position the project as design-stage. Keep the literature to one slide for this audience; the prelim version can expand it.
Prelim note
Expand to a method/year/author table ending with this project.

4. The question: which colleges should get the program first?

0.75 minprelim
Slide text
58 community college service areas cover North Carolina's 100 counties. A single-county pilot is moving to a statewide trial. Sudden unexpected death (SUD) incidence differs across the state.
Notes
Introduce Dr. Simpson's program, the education endpoint (an assessment of trained first responders and clinicians, averaged by college) and why incidence might guide allocation. The trial measures education, not SUD deaths.

2. Models

5. Spillover can reach only the controls, or everyone

1 minprelim
none (schematic of a treated college and its neighbors under the two regimes; to draw)
Slide text
Control-only spillover means untreated colleges benefit from treated neighbors. Both-arms spillover means every college responds to its neighbors' treatment. The best design depends on which one is true.
Notes
This is the single most important idea in the talk; return to it in every results slide. Exposure is the share of a college's neighbors that are treated.

6. We estimate the effect with a model that knows about neighbors

1 mintechnical
none (one equation in words, with an optional small equation)
Slide text
Outcome = direct effect of treatment + spillover from treated neighbors + spatial correlation + noise. A spatial lag model estimates the direct effect. We judge each design by its average error (MSE) and its error under an unlucky allocation.
Notes
Keep the math to a sentence for this audience. Mention that the model includes the spillover term, which is a best case. Define MSE as average squared distance between the estimate and the truth.
Prelim note
Show the equation Y = (I − ρW)^{-1}[τZ + S(Z) + ε] and both spillover forms.

3. Simulation study and designs

7. Nine ways to choose which clusters to treat

1.25 minprelim
Slide text
Simple random sampling (SRS) is the default. Others balance incidence (Balanced Quartiles), target it (High Incidence Focus), separate treated clusters (Checkerboard, Isolation Buffer, 2×2 Blocking) or vary the treated share by region (Saturation Regions, Incidence-Guided Saturation).
Notes
Walk through two or three panels only. Saturation designs treat 80, 60, 40 and 20 percent of four regions; the incidence-guided version gives the highest share to the highest-incidence region.

8. We tested them on a 100-cluster grid under many conditions

0.75 mintechnical
none (small parameter table)
Slide text
Three ways incidence varies across space, four strengths of spatial correlation, four spillover sizes, two spillover regimes, five effect sizes. 250 simulated trials per scenario.
Notes
One sentence on why a grid first. It lets us vary conditions systematically before moving to the real map.
Prelim note
Add queen versus rook contiguity, the oracle and non-oracle fits and the seed design.

9. On the grid, the spillover regime decides which design wins

1.5 minprelim
Slide text
Spillover to controls only means the saturation designs had about 37% lower error than SRS. Spillover to everyone means SRS was as good as any design, and the saturation designs were 4–8% worse.
Notes
Each point compares a design with SRS over 50 independent units; filled points are significant after multiple-comparison adjustment. Checkerboard and 2×2 Blocking look fine under one regime and fail badly under the other. Alternative figure if a simpler view is wanted is grid_accuracy_srs.png.

4. NC application

10. SUD incidence in NC is uneven, and the pattern shifts year to year

1 minprelim
Slide text
SUD deaths per 100,000 adults aged 18–64 by college service area, 2018–2021. Each year is a separate planning input.
Notes
23,523 deaths over 25.6 million person-years, from Habib's corrected county counts (Gan et al. case definition). Incidence guides who is treated; it does not enter the education outcome.

11. Each design was adapted to the real map before we looked at results

0.75 minprelim
Slide text
Four fixed regions for the saturation designs. A graph version of Checkerboard. Treated budgets differ, and we report them rather than force them equal.
Notes
Mention that regions were chosen for compactness and balance without looking at outcomes. regions.png is an alternative figure.

12. With all 58 colleges, saturation beats SRS when spillover reaches only controls

1 minprelim
Slide text
Spillover to controls only means Incidence-Guided Saturation had 21–30% lower error than SRS, depending on the year. Spillover to everyone means SRS and several designs were about equal.
Notes
Each cell is a design's error divided by SRS's in the same year and regime; blue is better than SRS. Same message as the grid.

13. Saturation also protects against an unlucky allocation

1 minprelim
Slide text
A trial gets one allocation. Under control-only spillover, most saturation allocations beat the average SRS allocation, and the worst 10% were 21–43% better than SRS's worst 10%.
Notes
The worst-decile estimates are uncertain because only ten sampled allocations form the worst decile. Under both-arms spillover the tail differences are small and noisy.

14. About 35 colleges detect a one-standard-deviation effect under spillover to everyone

1.25 minprelim
Slide text
Spillover to everyone means 35–36 colleges for 80% power with any design except Checkerboard and Isolation Buffer. Spillover to controls only means even 58 colleges are not enough at that effect; at 1.5 standard deviations the saturation designs need 27–28 colleges, against 31 for SRS.
Notes
Effects are in college-level standard deviations. For 25 trained professionals per college and an intraclass correlation of 0.05, a one-SD college effect is about 0.3 SD for an individual; d = 0.3 gives power 0.71 with 29 colleges and 0.96 with 58 under spillover to everyone. These numbers use a small-sample t test that keeps the false-positive rate at 5%.

15. If fewer colleges join, saturation's advantage shrinks

1 minprelim
Slide text
With 58 colleges the saturation designs have 22% lower error than SRS under control-only spillover. With 29 colleges, 4–5%. With 20, about 1%. Under control-only spillover, adding colleges past about 40 helps little.
Notes
When nearly every college joins, nearly every control has a treated neighbor, so spillover is hard to separate from treatment. Non-participating neighbors restore some contrast. If high-incidence colleges are more likely to volunteer, the advantage at 20–29 colleges is 2% or less. Ask the audience how many colleges they expect to join.

16. Incidence guidance redirects treatment only where regions differ

1 minprelim
Slide text
On the NC map, Incidence-Guided Saturation treats colleges with 51% of the incidence share, against 50% for plain saturation. On the grid, where regions differ more, the gain is 2–3 percentage points and grows with the regional spread.
Notes
NC's four regions have similar average incidence. Death share runs the other way because the highest-rate colleges are small (High Incidence Focus reaches 62% of rate share but 35% of deaths). Guidance costs no accuracy, so it is a reasonable ethical choice, but it should not be oversold on this map.

5. Conclusions, limitations, next steps

17. The best design depends mainly on how spillover travels

1 minprelim
none (take-home layout: claim, highlight box, three bullets)
Slide text
Highlight box: choose the design for the spillover you expect. Bullets: saturation when spillover reaches mainly controls; SRS or balanced designs when it reaches everyone; about 35 colleges detect a one-SD effect under spillover to everyone.
Notes
No single recommended design. Incidence-Guided Saturation matches plain saturation's accuracy while sending more treatment to high-burden regions, when regions differ.

18. What these results do not tell us

0.75 minprelim
none (two columns: limitations, future work)
Slide text
Limitations: the model knows the spillover form; planning incidence is treated as exact; contiguity stands in for professional networks. Future work: a future-incidence endpoint, noisy incidence, effect heterogeneity.
Notes
Mention that the results held when we fitted a CAR model or a Bayesian model (backup B4) and that a small-sample interval fixes the slight undercoverage (backup B2).

19. What we would like from you

0.75 mintalk-only
none
Slide text
Do you expect spillover to reach mainly untreated colleges, or everyone? How many colleges are likely to join, and would high-incidence colleges be more likely to? How many professionals per college, and how variable is the education score within a college?
Notes
These three answers decide the design and the sample size. Thank Dr. Simpson, Ashkan Habib and Dr. Lin.

Backup

B1. Formal tests agree with the descriptive ranking, with SRS included

technical
Slide text
Friedman test across six designs and SRS on 160 grid blocks, χ² = 560, df 6. Incidence-Guided Saturation ranks first; SRS and Balanced Quartiles cannot be separated.
Notes
Question it answers is "Are the design differences statistically significant?"

B2. A small-sample t interval restores nominal coverage

technical
none (table from Appendix A9, coverage by number of colleges)
Slide text
Wald tests reject a true null 11–13% of the time with 15 colleges and 6–7% with 58. The corrected t test rejects 4.4–5.6% at every size, with coverage 94–96%.
Notes
Answers "Why was coverage below 95%, and can it be fixed?"

B3. From a college-level effect to trained professionals

prelim
none (table tab:nc-translation)
Slide text
σ_c = √(ICC + (1 − ICC)/m). With m = 25 and ICC = 0.05, σ_c ≈ 0.30.
Notes
Answers "What does an effect of one standard deviation mean in practice?"

B4. The guidance holds under CAR and Bayesian models

technical
none (table tab:nc-bayes)
Slide text
CAR fitting or CAR data leave saturation at 0.76–0.82 of SRS's error under control-only spillover. A Bayesian spatial lag model reproduces the maximum likelihood results. Only a Bayesian CAR fitted to strongly correlated spatial lag data loses the saturation advantage.
Notes
Answers "Did you try a Bayesian model?" Cite Leroux et al. 2000, Lee 2013 (CARBayes) and LeSage and Pace 2009 on the slide.

B5. Rate share and death share pull apart in NC

prelim
none (table of rate share and death share by design)
Slide text
High Incidence Focus treats 62% of the rate share but 35% of deaths, because high-rate colleges are small.
Notes
Answers "Does incidence-guided allocation reach more deaths?"

B6. Checkerboard fails for different reasons on the grid and the map

technical
Slide text
Under queen contiguity, Checkerboard's estimates are unbiased but imprecise under control-only spillover. Under rook contiguity, the effect is not identified.
Notes
Answers "Why does strict alternation do so badly?"

B7. Binary spillover makes Isolation Buffer unidentifiable

technical
none (table tab:nc-forms)
Slide text
If any treated neighbor counts the same as all, every Isolation Buffer control is exposed, so the effect cannot be separated.
Notes
Answers "What if spillover is all-or-nothing?"

B8. Unequal college sizes cost power equally for every design

prelim
none
Slide text
Letting the number of trained professionals grow with college size lowers power by about 0.1 for every design and changes no design's standing.
Notes
Answers "What if colleges train different numbers of professionals?"
